slide.title: Episteme
slide.sub: A flight recorder for AI-assisted research

beats.say: Meet Episteme: a flight recorder for AI-assisted research.

slide.title: Episteme
slide.sub: A flight recorder for AI-assisted research

beats.say: It records what was planned, what was run, what happened, and why the approach changed. While the work happens, not afterwards.
You install two hooks: one in Claude Code, and one in git. From then on, every instruction, command, result and commit is captured automatically, into a raw log on your own machine.
Episteme groups that stream into episodes, and turns each one into a short diary of decisions: plans, runs, surprises, and changes of approach.

slide.title: Every entry points back to its *evidence*
slide.body: The raw log keeps everything the hooks saw, grouped into episodes. The diary keeps what a reviewer needs.

beats.say: The raw log keeps everything. The diary keeps only what a reviewer needs, and every diary entry points back to the raw evidence behind it.

slide.title: A study, step by step
slide.body: Demo study: predicting 30-day hospital readmission from clinical notes.

beats.say: Here's what that looks like, on a demo study that predicts hospital readmission from clinical notes.

slide.title: The expectation, stated *up front*
slide.body: The researcher expects AUROC ≥ 0.75 before anything runs.

beats.say: Step one: the researcher's plan, with an expectation stated up front. An AUROC of at least 0.75.

slide.title: The agent runs the *baseline*
slide.body: The run is captured with its command and its result: AUROC 0.54.

beats.say: Step two: the agent runs a baseline. The result is 0.54.

slide.title: Contradictions are caught *automatically*
slide.body: Episteme compares every result with the expectation before it, and records the surprise itself.

beats.say: Step three: Episteme notices, on its own, that the result contradicts the expectation, and records a surprise. Nobody had to write it down.

slide.title: A change of approach asks *why*
slide.body: The rules flag the pivot and ask for the reason, in the researcher's own words.

beats.say: Step four is the change of approach. Episteme's rules flag it, and ask for the reason, in the researcher's own words.
If a language model is connected, it proposes the reason, but only as a word-for-word quote of what was said at the time. Anything it can't quote is marked as inferred, and never presented as fact.

slide.title: One click to *confirm*
slide.body: The reason is on the record, linked to the surprise that triggered it.

beats.say: The researcher confirms it with one click. Now the reason is on the record, linked to the surprise that triggered it.
Every entry carries a badge: stated by the researcher, stated by the agent, or inferred by Episteme's own rules. So a reviewer always knows how much weight each line can bear.

slide.title: What was *actually run*
slide.body: Command, parameters, result and status, captured from the run itself.

beats.say: Open any run, and you see what was actually executed: the command, its parameters, and its result.

slide.title: One click to the *raw capture*
slide.body: The exact output the hook recorded, including the line the result came from.

beats.say: And one click further, the raw capture it came from.

slide.title: Ask the log
slide.body: Someone who wasn't there asks the question from the start of this video.

beats.say: Now, the reviewer who wasn't there can simply ask the log.

slide.title: An answer that *cites* the record
slide.body: The reason, who stated it, and what triggered it. Answers cite only diary entries.

beats.say: Why did they change approach at step four? The answer comes back with citations: the reason, stated by the researcher, and the surprise that triggered it. Answers cite only entries in the diary, so there is no invented history.

slide.title: The decision record, *ready for the paper*

beats.say: When it's time to publish, export the record as a Markdown decision appendix for your paper, or as W3C PROV-JSON for provenance tools.
